The Pentagon is pressing U.S. defense companies to rapidly boost weapons production after the Iran war sharply depleted missile stocks.
Firms have 21 days to propose faster deliveries, expanded factories, and increased capacity.
The biggest concern is air-defense ammunition: Patriot inventories reportedly fell from about 2,200 to under 827, while THAAD stocks dropped from 452 to under 278. 
The Pentagon is pursuing major production deals, including a $58.6 billion Lockheed Martin agreement, but much of the expansion depends on a $1.15 trillion defense spending bill stalled in Congress.
Source: WaPo

Its effectiveness is limited by Starlink’s rapidly moving satellite network, while its large footprint and strong emissions make it relatively easy to detect and target.

🇹🇷 Turkey’s quiet Black Sea shipping squeeze – what if it becomes permanent?
 
🔴 The Turkish authority responsible for the monitoring and management of heavy commercial cargoes through the Bosporus and the Dardanelles has reportedly started restricting the passage of vessels bound to and from Russian and Ukrainian ports.
🔴 Sources told Bloomberg the Directorate General of Coastal Safety has implemented de facto restrictions by halting the issuance of transit permits, or deliberately dragging out the review of applications. Ships bound for Turkish, Bulgarian, Romanian and Georgian ports are being allowed to proceed as normal.
🔴 The restrictions come in the wake of a series of drone attacks on Turkish-flagged and owned vessels, plus the targeting of Russian compressor stations linked to TurkStream and Blue Stream gas pipeline infrastructure. Up to 10 crew members have been killed and 7 injured in the last month.
 
Implications
 
➡️ the restrictions stretch the limits of Turkey’s legal authority under the 1936 Montreux Convention, which guarantees “absolute freedom of navigation” for commercial vessels. If they become permanent, that opens the door for other countries in command of natural or manmade maritime passages doing the same (Egypt, Panama, Spain, Iran, Yemen, Indonesia-Malaysia-Singapore, Chile, South Africa, Russia)
➡️ while the restrictions could hurt Russian energy and food exporters, they may absolutely cripple Ukraine, which has no alternative major maritime export routes
➡️ Kazak crude exports (80% of which pass through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal at Novorossiysk) may also be severely affected. There are no viable, large-scale alternatives
➡️ a block on Russian energy exports will exacerbate the global energy crisis caused by the Iran war – pummeling net importers, especially if shipping restrictions are complemented by a shutdown of Turkey-bound natural gas exports, which besides Turkey also feed much of southeastern Europe
➡️ the Black Sea region accounts for up to 20% of global grain exports, 60% of sunflower oil exports, and 15% or more of global mineral fertilizer exports. Unless costly alternative overland routes are found, entire regions and subcontinents, from North Africa to the Middle East, could plunge into economic and political crises

🤥🇮🇷 Trump’s Iran brinksmanship painting him into a corner – and the US out of the Gulf
 
Trump may have believed his own hype, betting that restarting the Iran war would finally deliver the quick victory that eluded him the first time. Instead, Tehran now threatens to hand to hand Washington a defeat even more humiliating than the one delineated in the June 17 Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).
While the MoU did not include explicit clauses that would strip the US military of its right to navigate Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, Iranian officials’ latest terms in talks with Oman include demands that US Navy warships stay out of the area completely.
💬 “The fundamental result is going to be significant Iranian de facto control over the Strait,” former US intel officer Jonathan Panikoff told WSJ.
US officials insist Washington will not accept any deal which allows Iran to collect tolls, or deny access to the Strait.
But given the vast arsenal the IRGC has its disposal to target violating vessels, Washington doesn’t seem to have much leverage in the matter. American warship and carrier strikes groups have already kept well away from the Iranian coastline throughout t the war, fearing ballistic, cruise missile and drone strikes.
Gulf officials have reportedly “acknowledged” that de facto Iranian control over the Strait may be the new normal, and the “best option,” given the impact of its continued closure on global energy markets and regional economies.
 
🤔 History in the making?
 
A US retreat from the Gulf would set back US policy in the region 55 years – back to the 1971 basing agreement with Bahrain, and subsequent[ expansions to bases across Arab Gulf countries.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73010) Iran’s counterstrikes since February showed that these bases are not only defenseless, but pointless when it comes to the protection of America’s Gulf allies. On the contrary – the more US bases a country hosts, the more vulnerable it is to Iranian strikes.
President Masoud Pezeshkian reiterated Friday that Iran would do everything in its power to prevent the US and Israel from uniting the Gulf countries against it – starting with the reminder that unlike Israel, Iran has “no intention of attacking other countries, seizing territory or expanding our borders.”

🇮🇱🔍 Why Israeli politicians are desperate to shut Palestinians out of power
Israel's opposition once argued that cooperation with Palestinian Arab parties was key to ending Benjamin Netanyahu's long dominance of Israeli politics.
Now, the same politicians are trying to freeze Palestinian Arabs out of the government, despite the fact that they represent one-fifth of the population.
The pledge has been repeated in recent weeks by figures across the anti-Netanyahu camp, such as Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, who used to defend their partnership with Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas as the necessary price of ending Netanyahu’s dominance.
The same stance is shared by Gadi Eisenkot, who has been positioning himself as a potential PM. Opinion polls suggest that at the October election Eisenkot's bloc will be running neck-and-neck with Netanyahu's coalition.
👉 This marks a sharp retreat from the pragmatic experiment of 2021 and shows how the events of October 2023 rewired the political climate around cooperation with Palestinian citizens of Israel.
The latter make up roughly two million people and are descendants of those who remained after the 1948 war.
Their parties have sat on the political margins for decades, and the taboo was broken only in 2021, when Ra’am’s four seats allowed Bennett and Lapid to assemble a majority.
However, that arrangement lasted barely a year. Now, the taboo appears to have returned.
🔴 71.5% of Jewish Israelis oppose including Arab parties in the next government (Israel Democracy Institute)
🔴 57% of Israelis oppose a Palestinian state under any circumstances (Institute for National Security Studies survey)
Political arithmetic may ultimately prove more stubborn than campaign rhetoric since Israel's fragmented parliament has repeatedly produced deadlocks.
Recent polling suggests neither bloc can count on securing a majority alone.
There is also another lingering question: whether the political cost of ignoring Palestinian citizens of Israel will eventually become too high for the Zionist state.

🇮🇱🇸🇾 Israel's Syrian land grab: bulldozers, drones, and heavy machine guns
Israeli forces have carried out 20 incursions in Deraa and Quneitra in just the past week, conducting land-clearing operations, erecting checkpoints, and installing surveillance cameras, the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reports. 
Israeli troops also entered populated areas, firing heavy machine guns toward agricultural lands.
The strategic picture:
➡️ Israel is expanding its occupation of Syrian territory — including the Golan Heights, a UN buffer zone, and Mount Hermon — while bombing Syria's air defenses
➡️ Netanyahu has boasted that he helped install Syrian terrorist-turned-President Ahmed al-Sharaa (former HTS leader Abu Mohammad al-Julani) in power in Damascus
➡️ Sharaa's forces refuse to confront Israeli incursions — instead targeting Alawite and Druze minorities, including major massacres in March and July
SOHR warned that Israel is "creating new realities on the ground and gradually altering the border strip" in the absence of any international measures to deter violations and respect Syrian sovereignty.
Israel is occupying Syria to control its water resources and expand Greater Israel — and Damascus is letting it happen.

🇸🇦🛢 Beyond the Gulf: How Saudi oil disruption is testing global markets
US imports of Saudi crude fell to zero in July for the first time since 1985, according to preliminary Department of Energy data. For a country that was importing more than 800,000 barrels a day from Saudi Arabia, that is a striking reversal.
The immediate problem is geography. The war with Iran has turned the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf’s main oil artery, into a major risk zone. Saudi Arabia can bypass Hormuz through its Red Sea terminals, but that route is also under pressure from the renewed conflict with the Houthis, which the kingdom itself helped reignite, leaving its exports exposed on both sides.
🤔 The missing Saudi barrels are therefore more than a supply story. They show how quickly geopolitical confrontation can disrupt an oil system.
For US refiners, that means finding heavy crude elsewhere. Venezuelan shipments have risen sharply, from roughly 100,000 barrels a day in January to nearly 600,000 in July. But Venezuela is hardly the winner here: Washington spent years sanctioning and restricting its oil industry, only to turn back to Venezuelan barrels as disruptions elsewhere tightened supply.
Saudi Arabia is having to adjust too, offering Asian buyers a $2-per-barrel discount against the Oman-Dubai benchmark for next month, a sign that disrupted trade routes are forcing even one of the world’s biggest oil exporters to compete harder for buyers.
The bigger story is not simply that Saudi barrels disappeared from the US market. It is that the oil system is being forced to reroute around multiple political and military crises at once.
👉 Washington spent decades trying to shape who produces oil, who sells it, and where it flows. Riyadh spent years projecting military power across its neighborhood. Now both are being reminded of an inconvenient rule of energy geopolitics: you can pressure countries, sanction producers, and wage wars, but tankers still need a safe route from A to B.
That is what makes the current disruption bigger than the Gulf itself. If both Hormuz and the Red Sea remain under pressure, global oil flows will keep shifting, freight and insurance costs will rise, and refiners will compete harder for replacement barrels.
The world is not running out of oil. The problem is increasingly whether the oil can get where it needs to go without passing through someone else’s war.

🇯🇵 Is Japan about to outsource its military kill chain to Palantir's genocide-coded AI?
Japan is on the brink of surrendering military decision-making to the surveillance-tech powerhouse that orchestrates the Pentagon’s AI-driven kill chain.
[It is mulling plugging](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71402) Palantir’s [Maven Smart System](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71058) and Anduril’s Lattice into the command-and-control structure of its Self-Defense Forces (SDF), Nikkei Asia reports.
👉 Separate platforms are to be assigned to counterattacks, missile defense, and drone control.
Right now, the SDF runs zero AI in its command structure, while the US military already [runs Maven to gorge ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71084)on battlefield data, letting its algorithms play God with target selection.
Currently, Japanese decision-making is slower than the Pentagon’s, raising fears that the gap could undermine interoperability with US forces.
The increased speed will come at a cost:
🔶 classified Japanese military information would be fed into software built by a foreign company
🔶 Even if the data centers remain on Japanese soil, its military would still depend on the US corporations for software updates, system capabilities and long-term support
Japanese officials claim they can later swap the foreign tech for domestic AI, but for now, reliance on US systems is treated as unavoidable if capabilities are to be raised quickly.
The shortcut comes with plenty of despicable baggage.
🔴 Maven was unleashed with wrecking-ball gusto in the US war on Iran
🔴 It fuses satellite imagery, drone feeds, radar, sensors and intel into targeting options with speed over precision
🔴 Maven reportedly gets target classification right only 60% of the time (well below human analysts' 84%)
🔴 Most notably, it was linked to the deadly American[ Tomahawk strike on a girls’ school in Iran’s Minab.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/68059)
Palantir, which post-October 2023 supplied Israel with systems like Lavender and Gospel to automatically generate battlefield kill lists, was blacklisted from public entities by Spain.
France, Germany, and the UK have ended intelligence contracts.
Plugging Palantir into the SDF would be another step toward tighter fusion with the US-led military machine as Japan hurtles toward a [more militarized future.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71510)
